comments.author: @therainman7777
comments.text:
No offense to Sabine, but this is not her main area of expertise. She’s a physicist who comments on AI on her YouTube channel, but I don’t think she is more knowledgeable about the potential growth rates and limitations of current and future AI models than are AI engineers, researchers, and safety specialists who do this for a living and spend 100% of their time on it. These people are also working, behind the scenes, with the latest and most capable models and techniques which Sabine (and the public in general) do not yet have access to and are not even aware of yet.

One clear example of this is her confident belief that we will hit the “data wall” and be unable to develop AGI for that reason. However, this fully neglects the fact that not all AI methods require large amounts of static, pre-existing data. Techniques based on reinforcement learning, self-play, discrete program search, etc., are all viable potential paths to AGI and ASI, and they do not require vast amounts of training data. In fact, many of these techniques do not require any training data at all; see AlphaZero reaching superhuman levels in dozens of games with absolutely zero pre-existing training data.

Exponential growth is described in the context of AI learning from machine learning papers written by other AI systems, 51:00  however, this growth is ultimately limited by the incorporeal nature of AI, which prevents it from truly recognizing the most valuable signals. As AI systems generate more content, the amount of irrelevant or misleading information increases at a similar rate to the useful information. This makes it difficult for the signal (useful information) to stand out from the noise (irrelevant information). Humans are required to navigate AI assertions to identify and extract corporeal value, that is the limiting factor of the growth rate, along with differing opinions of good signal.

In the early days of the internet, Google's search engine made the best information easily discoverable. However, as new websites emerged, they began to identify patterns for optimizing their search rankings, prioritizing these patterns over providing the most useful information. This led to a proliferation of websites with less valuable content that outranked the better information, ultimately reducing the overall quality of search results.

This phenomenon is a combination of Campbell's law, which states that when change is driven by measurements, those measurements will be influenced to drive the desired change, and the Cobra Effect, where incentives intended to solve a problem can inadvertently make it worse. In the latter case, when authorities offer rewards for snake heads to reduce the snake population, it incentivizes people to breed snakes to collect the rewards, ultimately increasing the snake population instead of decreasing it.

The doom and gloom scenarios often associated with AI, such as the grey goo hypothesis or AI apocalypse, actually stem from the actions of those people who seek to influence measurements for their own gain (measurement influencers) and people who exploit incentive structures in unintended ways (snake farmers). These actors and similar, rather than the AI systems themselves, are the greatest threat to undesirable outcomes.

Besides, maybe someone like "Roko" telling people they would run the risk of being punished for not working towards the creation of superintelligence actually has unforeseeable consequences - for some the idea could freeze them with anxiety, ruining the possibility of the creativity they would have needed to make useful contributions towards the task.  

Even for a superintelligence, this would lead to the usual ad absurdum and ad infinitum problems. You could never know if people preventing something from happening actually was the best thing that could have happened to you. Maybe if the creation of the superintelligence had been on track to be created a decade earlier, the beating of the wing of a butterfly which have triggered a hurricane would have meant that the key leading scientists would have been on a plane for a conference in Florida and would all have been killed in a crash, meaning it would not have been created at all! No one - even a superintelligence - can know what WOULD have happened if something in the past had been different, just like with the beating of the wing of a butterfly being able to trigger a hurricane.  

Anyone who has ever thought "I wonder how my life would have been different if..." can attest to the fog of unknowables which quickly multiply as one tries to analyze one's life story with this hypothetical in mind.

It's difficult to know what a qualitatively different intelligence would be like, psychologically, but one would hope it would not play such neurotic victim-games, given that it has access to all the literature of the philosophers and great spiritual traditions.
